newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Japan set on financial "Big Bang" - MOF official.
newsitem.headline: Japan set on financial "Big Bang" - MOF official.

text.p: Japan will carry out promised "Big Bang" financial reforms despite the inate conservatism of both government and bureaucrats, a senior Japanese finance ministry official said on Wednesday.

"Although we generally prefer the gradualist approach to shock therapy, we are now determined to implement the shock therapy in this particular field," said Eisuke Sakakibara, director general of the ministry's International Finance Bureau.

"I for one will spearhead this move by submitting the draft of the revision of the Foreign Exchange Control Act, which would completely deregulate foreign exchange transactions in Tokyo, in the next normal session of the Diet," Sakakibara said during a panel discussion at the World Economic Forum in Hong Kong.
Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto last week unveiled a plan to liberalise Japan's financial markets to catch up with reforms carried out years ago in Europe and North America.
The proposal has been widely welcomed, but many analysts and foreign business executives have expressed scepticism about whether it could be successfully carried out.
Sakakibara, known as "Mr Yen" because of his influence on foreign exchange policy, said he understood their doubts.
"Knowing the gradualist approach that the Ministry of Finance (MOF) has taken for the last 20 years, this is a reasonable sort of scepticism," he said.
But the Hashimoto government has staked its survival on carrying out the proposals, he said.

"Finance Minister (Hiroshi) Mitsuzuka said he was determined to push it through. He expects bullets to be shot at him from behind and the side. He might be shot, but he said he is prepared for that," he said.
"So the political determination is there, and the Ministry of Finance, conservative organisation as it is, would follow that political initiative in a whole-hearted manner."
Sakakibara acknowledged that, on top of the ministry's conservatism, Hashimoto headed a conservative government.

"But if you look back to history, it may be the so-called reformers or the liberals who start talking about the reforms, but it is usually the conservatives who implement the radical reforms," he said.
Japanese business executives on Tuesday said they too believed reforms and deregulation would be carried out this time after years of talk because public sentiment was now solidly behind the effort.

"I think the experience of real economic stalemate we suffered as a result of the bubble economy (bursting) changed the entire social perception about the need of reform and deregulation," Toyoo Gyohten, senior advisor to the Bank of Tokyo-Mitsubishi, said at the World Economic Forum.
But the businessmen agreed reforms would not be easy.

"The anti-reform faction in our system, which is often called the iron-triangle of bureaucrats, business and politicians, is still very, very powerful," said Hatsuhisa Takashima, executive controller general of Japan Broadcasting Corp (NHK).
